description:
Fire in space. AI. NASA data. One big question: how does fire behave in microgravity, and can we predict what happens next?

We're building Flame in Freefall for NASA Space Apps Challenge and looking for teammates with skills in Python, AI/ML, data science, data analysis, scientific research, web development or UI/UX design.

Got skills, ideas, or a love for solving hard problems? Join us. Let's build something worth showing off.

Wanna join the winning team? 👀
summary:
FireTrace is an interactive research platform that transforms NASA's microgravity combustion data into accessible, evidence-based insights.

We analysed experimental data from FLEX, BASS-II, SAME-R and SAFFIRE-I, covering liquid-fuel combustion, solid materials, smoke behaviour and spacecraft fire experiments.

Our five-page website combines an interactive Experiment Lab, scientific plots, transparent evidence ranking, traceable research findings and machine-learning model validation. Ask FireTrace, our Gemini-powered research assistant, lets users explore scientific questions in everyday language, supported by NASA evidence and citations.

Beyond visualisation, we evaluated models for predicting extinction droplet diameter, burning constant, burn time and experimental outcomes. An expanded model search reduced average extinction-diameter prediction error by 15.4% in repeated grouped validation.

We clearly distinguish measured data from calculated results, AI explanations and illustrative animations.

FireTrace addresses the challenge by making complex combustion research easier to explore, compare and understand, supporting future research into fire safety during human space exploration.
details:
Our approach

FireTrace was built to make NASA's extensive microgravity combustion research easier to access, interpret and compare. Rather than creating another static dashboard or a general-purpose chatbot, we developed a connected research environment that brings experimental data, scientific analysis, evidence ranking and exploratory prediction together.

1. Data preparation and scientific analysis

We collected and processed NASA investigation data from FLEX, BASS-II, SAME-R and SAFFIRE-I.

Our analysis includes 274 FLEX droplet-combustion records, 129 BASS-II solid-material records and 109 SAME-R smoke/aerosol records, alongside spacecraft-fire sensor and telemetry streams from SAFFIRE-I.

We cleaned and structured the data, documented variables and measurement units, preserved missing values and maintained links to original sources. We also accounted for important differences between independent experiments and repeated sensor measurements.

2. Five connected research features

  • Experiment Lab: Users can select recorded experiments, inspect conditions and outcomes, and explore an illustrative flame animation. The animation is educational, not a validated combustion simulation.
  • Scientific Plots: Interactive graphs allow users to filter measurements and examine relationships involving fuel, oxygen, pressure and combustion outcomes.
  • Evidence Ranking: A transparent scoring system helps identify which investigations are most relevant to a research objective. These are research-relevance rankings, not certified safety-risk predictions.
  • Sources & Findings: Findings are linked to original NASA investigations, making their evidence and limitations easier to trace.
  • Model Validation: We compare machine-learning predictions against experimental results, displaying errors, model performance and individual test cases.

3. Gemini-powered scientific assistant

Ask FireTrace integrates Google Gemini with a local scientific evidence engine. The engine retrieves relevant NASA measurements, calculations and source references. Gemini uses this evidence to generate explanations in natural language.

This allows users to ask questions about combustion behaviour, experimental differences and scientific findings without manually searching through large datasets.

Our design separates verified evidence from AI-generated explanations and identifies uncertainty where the available data cannot support a conclusion.

4. Machine-learning validation

We developed four separate predictive targets: extinction droplet diameter, burning constant, burn time and test-end category.

We compared candidate models using grouped cross-validation to reduce leakage between experiments with similar conditions.

The expanded model search reduced mean extinction-diameter error from 0.434 mm to 0.367 mm, a 15.4% improvement across repeated validation. Burning-constant and burn-time prediction errors also decreased.

We report errors transparently and acknowledge that the previously inspected fixed test set is not fresh independent validation. These models are exploratory and are not certified for spacecraft fire-safety decisions.

5. Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with interactive scientific visualisations.
  • Backend: Node.js, TypeScript and Express.
  • Data processing: Python, pandas, structured JSON and scientific data-validation scripts.
  • Artificial intelligence: Google Gemini through the Gemini API, grounded in prepared NASA evidence.
  • Machine learning: Regression, tree-ensemble methods and grouped model validation.
  • Storage and reliability: SQLite for request accounting, caching and rate limits; automated tests.
  • Development and deployment: Git, GitHub, Google Antigravity, OpenAI Codex, Render and Railway.

Creativity and intended impact

FireTrace's strength is its evidence-first approach. It connects experiments, interactive explanations, AI-assisted research and measurable model performance while keeping scientific limitations visible.

The intended users include students, researchers and people exploring fire safety for future space missions.

Rather than claiming to predict spacecraft fires, FireTrace provides a foundation for understanding existing experimental evidence, identifying relevant research and exploring questions that warrant further investigation.
